Deal-level intelligence · v0.1

Who gets to own Quebec infrastructure.

Quebec is building the largest energy expansion in its history, and its mid-market is changing hands. Most of the record sits in French: Régie de l'énergie dockets, Hydro-Québec tender results, provincial decrees. Almost no one on Bay Street or in New York reads it.

This tracker reads those filings and publishes them in structured English. Every figure carries its source and a confidence flag R-4227-2023. Where a number is sealed, it says so rather than estimating.

Pipeline, not yet financed

Quebec announces capacity years before it reaches financial close. That gap is public, it is written in French, and it is where the next decade of project finance mandates will come from.

04

Method

What gets recorded

Sponsor and sponsor type, asset and asset type, capacity, province, stage, offtake counterparty and tenor, rating, acquirer origin and capital source. Each field carries its own source and date, not one citation for the whole row.

The disclosure cliff

Privatization is itself a disclosure event. When a Quebec issuer goes private, its filings stop and its press archive is often pruned. Innergex now retains five press items and no investor section. Boralex will follow at close. This tracker records the last public state of an asset before that happens, because afterward no amount of searching recovers it.

What does not

Per-developer PPA pricing, debt tranche margins, mezzanine terms and mid-market multiples are sealed or redacted in Quebec filings. They are marked confidential rather than estimated. Guessing at them would make the whole database less useful than admitting the limit.

Confidence flags

Disclosed stated by a party or a regulator. Reported from credible secondary press, not yet confirmed in a filing. Confidential exists but is sealed. Unverified carried from secondary reporting and not yet confirmed in a primary document. Shown so the gap stays visible.

Primary sources

  • Régie de l'énergie dockets, decisions
  • Hydro-Québec appels d'offres, Plan 2035
  • DBRS Morningstar rating reports
  • SEDAR+ issuer filings
  • Canada Infrastructure Bank participations
  • BAPE hearings, decrees
05

Notes

Short pieces published when the data says something the consensus does not.

No. 3 · August 2026

Hydro-Québec is funding the 2035 plan with 40-year bonds, and every Canadian dealer is in the syndicate.

On 7 August, Hydro-Québec reopened its Series JU bonds for another C$500M. The coupon is 4.00%, priced at 84.479 to yield 4.900%, maturing in February 2065. This was the seventeenth reopening of a line first issued in September 2024. That series now stands at C$9.0B on its own.

The syndicate is worth reading. RBC led. National Bank and TD were co-leads. BMO, CIBC, Scotia, Desjardins, Laurentian and Casgrain filled out the book. Every major Canadian dealer is underwriting this, which follows when one provincial utility is carrying a 10,000 MW wind target plus the transmission to move the power.

It also shows where private capital does not fit. Hydro-Québec borrows for forty years in the public market at terms no project sponsor can match. Private money enters further down the structure: developer equity, partnership stakes, and the project debt behind tenders like A/O 2026-01, where bids close in February.

No. 2 · August 2026

Transurban spent three years exiting the A25. La Caisse bought both halves.

Transurban, an Australian toll-road operator, sold half of the A25 concession to La Caisse in 2023. In June 2026 it sold the rest for C$280M in equity. Operations moved to Plenary Americas, which La Caisse also owns. A foreign investor is now completely out of one of only two public-private tolled highways in Quebec, and the provincial fund owns all of it and runs it through its own operator.

Boralex followed the same path with more steps visible. La Caisse has been both a shareholder and a lender there since 2017. In July 2025, it and Fondaction put C$250M of subordinated debt into the company. Eight months later it agreed to take Boralex private alongside Brookfield, rolling its stake from roughly 15% to 30%. Lender, then shareholder, then owner.

Put those next to Innergex and the pattern is hard to miss. Outside capital is not being kept out. It is being bought out in stages, on friendly terms, by an institution with a longer horizon and a mandate that is not only financial.

For anyone lending to or investing in Quebec infrastructure, the question is not whether you can get in. It is what your exit looks like, and who will be buying when you want one.

No. 1 · August 2026

Outside capital is not taking over Quebec's mid-market. It is being bought out.

The easy story is that foreign money is pouring into Quebec. The transactions say otherwise, and Innergex is the clearest example. Before the take-private, Hydro-Québec already held about 19.9% and CDPQ was the second largest shareholder, having first invested in 1995. CDPQ then bought the rest at C$13.75 a share, an enterprise value of C$10.0B, and syndicated up to 20% of what it had invested to Investissement Québec, Desjardins Global Asset Management and Fondaction, along with 14 Swiss institutions. Foreign capital was not excluded. It was admitted at a size someone else chose.

Boralex followed the same logic. Brookfield did not buy around La Caisse, it bought with La Caisse, which rolled roughly 15% up to 30% of the private company, and the head office stays in Quebec. The C$1.8B eStruxture recapitalization brought in new capital while the Wener Family Office and the founding CEO reinvested rather than sold.

Where out-of-province buyers did take control, they did it in two places. Take-privates of listed companies, where a public bid cannot be quietly pre-empted. And digital infrastructure, where the domestic bench is thinner and the capital required is more than a provincial balance sheet wants to carry alone. Even those come with conditions. Blue Wolf and Stonepeak paid C$67.00 a share for Logistec in October 2023, and the announcement pairs a contemplated Investissement Québec participation with a commitment to keep the head office and operations in Quebec.

The next test is A/O 2026-01, with bids closing in February. Watch whether the winning consortia are led by domestic sponsors with foreign money behind them, and whether that shapes the financing structures that follow.
